bullets: Bombings, riots, checkpoints and armoured patrols were part of everyday life for civilians.
‘Belfast confetti’ was slang for shrapnel and missiles used in riots.
Checkpoint questions about **name and where you come from** could reveal religion/community, which could be dangerous.
Many Belfast streets were named after **British imperial victories**, including Crimean War battles, a reminder of Britain’s colonial history in Ireland.
Carson was also a traditional musician: rhythm and sound matter in his long lines.

callouts.p: Learn three short phrases from your anthology: the punctuation raining, the street names, and the final questions.

core.p: Ciaran Carson (1948–2019) was a Belfast poet, raised Irish-speaking in a Catholic family. Belfast Confetti appeared in The Irish for No (1987/1989). The **Troubles (late 1960s–1998)** was a violent conflict in Northern Ireland between mainly Catholic nationalists/republicans (who wanted a united Ireland) and mainly Protestant unionists/loyalists (who wanted to stay in the UK), with the British Army deployed on the streets.

bullets: **Conflict type**: civil/sectarian conflict; urban violence; individual vs state/military.
**Big message**: conflict breaks language, identity and freedom; civilians are trapped in a militarised city.
**Perspective**: first person, present-tense immediacy, a writer’s viewpoint.
core.p: Riot police move in and a bomb explodes, scattering metal like punctuation. The speaker’s thoughts are interrupted and he cannot complete a sentence. He tries to escape through streets he knows well, named after Crimean battles, but every route is blocked. He meets armoured vehicles and soldiers who demand his name and where he is from and going.

bullets: Stanza 1 = explosion; stanza 2 = attempted escape and interrogation.
Long lines with **caesura** and **enjambment** create breathless, chaotic movement.
Broken sentences show the speaker’s **disorientation**.
Ends in questions: no resolution, no escape.
The **extended metaphor** of punctuation unifies the poem.
core.p: **Two stanzas** of **free verse** with very long, irregular lines, heavy punctuation and broken syntax.

**Militarisation** and loss of freedom.

plan: Entrapment: the valley vs the labyrinth
essays.q: Compare how places are presented in Belfast Confetti and The Charge of the Light Brigade.
essays.text: Tennyson’s soldiers ride into a valley lined on three sides by guns, and the anaphora of ‘Cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them’ encloses them in the structure of the stanza. Carson’s speaker is also enclosed, but in his own city: he knows the streets intimately, yet every route is blocked, so familiarity offers no escape. The most striking link is in the names. Carson’s streets are named after Balaclava, Raglan and other Crimean battles, the very events Tennyson’s poem glorified, so the language of imperial victory has become the map of a modern conflict. Where Tennyson, writing as Poet Laureate, ends by commanding the nation to ‘Honour the Light Brigade’, Carson ends with a soldier’s rapid questions about his name and where he is going, which in the Troubles could reveal a person’s religion. Place, for Carson, is no longer a site of glory but of suspicion.
essays.thesis: Both poems trap people in a deadly place, and they are linked by the same names, but Tennyson’s valley is a stage for glory while Carson’s streets, named after that glory, have become a maze of everyday fear.
why: Uses the poems’ shared reference (Crimean names) for a perceptive link.
AO3 for both: Laureate; checkpoints in the Troubles.

poem.how: In copyright: open your anthology beside this guide. Two stanzas with very long lines; watch the punctuation.

stanzas.gist: Riot police move in and an explosion showers the street with metal: nuts, bolts, nails, car keys (the ‘confetti’ of the title). The speaker describes the debris as punctuation marks falling like rain. He is trying to finish a sentence in his head, but it keeps breaking up; the blast becomes an asterisk on a map, and gunfire becomes a line of hyphens.
stanzas.label: Stanza 1: the explosion

notes.n: ‘Belfast confetti’ was slang for the bits of metal (nuts, bolts, nails) thrown in riots or packed into bombs. **Irony**: confetti is for celebrations; here it is shrapnel.
**Extended metaphor**: shrapnel becomes punctuation marks. Violence literally breaks language; the speaker cannot speak or think clearly.
The speaker is a writer trying to form a sentence: **trauma disrupts communication**. The form performs this: broken syntax, caesura, dashes.
Each mark becomes a visual image of the blast (asterisk = explosion on a map, hyphens = bursts of fire, question marks = confusion). **Semantic field** of writing and print.
Very long lines with **lists** (nuts, bolts, nails, keys) are cluttered and overwhelming, like debris. **Asyndetic** listing speeds up the chaos.

stanzas.gist: The speaker knows this maze of streets intimately, yet he cannot get out: every alley is blocked. The streets carry the names of Crimean War battles and commanders (Balaclava, Raglan, Inkerman, Odessa). He is stopped by an armoured vehicle and soldiers in helmets and visors, who fire questions at him: his name, where he has come from, where he is going.
stanzas.label: Stanza 2: trapped in the streets

notes.n: **Metaphor**: the familiar city has become a maze with no exit. He knows it ‘like the back of his hand’ but is still trapped: home is no longer safe.
Real Belfast street names commemorating British imperial battles. **Irony and allusion**: history of war is written into the city; links to The Charge of the Light Brigade (Balaclava, Raglan).
notes.w: Crimean War street names (Balaclava, Raglan, Inkerman, Odessa)

notes.n: Every escape is closed off: entrapment, both physical and political.
Imagery of the **militarised city**: soldiers are faceless, dehumanised behind visors. Civilians live under occupation.

The poem ends in an **interrogation** at a checkpoint: the questions are literal (security checks) and existential (identity, past, future). In Northern Ireland, ‘where are you from’ could reveal your religion and community: a dangerous question.
notes.w: The final questions (name, where from, where to)

notes.n: The final image compares the soldiers’ questions to a burst of gunfire (a ‘fusillade’). Questions become weapons: the **extended metaphor** of language-as-violence ends the poem.

poem.title: Belfast Confetti

summary: Belfast Confetti (Ciaran Carson, 1989) describes a speaker caught in a riot and bomb explosion in Belfast during the Troubles, using punctuation as an extended metaphor for shrapnel and broken language; compare how it presents the chaos and fear of conflict, trapped identity and the militarised city, with the context of Northern Ireland.

terms.d: A metaphor sustained across the poem (punctuation as shrapnel).
A group of words linked by topic (writing and print).
Conflict between religious or political groups.
